blocks.text: Growth in plants is a permanent increase in size, which can occur in height, width and mass. Throughout its life the plant adds organs such as branches, leaves and roots; its organs grow from their tips, but the rate of growth is not uniform throughout the body. In lower plants the whole body can grow, but in higher plants growth is limited to growing points, groups of cells called meristems that are capable of continuous division.

items: Apical meristems are found at the tips of roots and shoots and are mainly responsible for the extension of the plant body. They are perpetual growth zones that increase the number of cells at the tips of roots and stems, and they play the key role in primary growth.

Intercalary meristems are separated from the apex by permanent tissues. They lie at the bases of internodes in many plants such as grasses, play an important part in producing leaves and flowers, and are temporary.

Lateral meristems are cylinders of dividing cells along the periphery, responsible for growth in the thickness of stems and roots. Found in woody plants, they are crucial for secondary growth and take two forms: the vascular cambium, between the xylem and phloem, which produces secondary xylem and secondary phloem; and the cork cambium, in the outer layer of stems and roots, which produces cork cells that replace the epidermis and form the protective outer bark.

blocks.text: Primary growth increases the length of the plant and is brought about by the apical meristems. Herbaceous plants generally show primary growth with little secondary growth compared with woody plants. Primary growth occurs in three phases.

items: Cell division: the cells of the apical meristems divide and the number of cells increases, at the tips of the root and shoot. This zone of cell division contains small, non-vacuolated cells with spherical nuclei at the centre of the cytoplasm.

Cell elongation: the new cells increase in volume by taking up water; the plasticity of the cell wall increases and wall pressure is reduced. This happens a little behind the tips, in the zone of cell elongation, where the cells are vacuolated and large with their nuclei at the periphery of the cytoplasm. Different cells elongate in different dimensions to reach their final size: cells destined to become pith or cortex do not elongate much lengthwise, while those destined to become xylem elongate much more.

Cell differentiation: once the cells have their final size and shape, elongation stops and they specialise for specific functions; their walls thicken and new structural features develop. This happens next to the zone of elongation, in the zone of cell differentiation, where each type of cell performs its specific function.

blocks.alt: A longitudinal section of a root tip. A colour bar marks, from the tip upward, the Zone of Division (blue), Zone of Elongation (green) and Zone of Differentiation (orange). blocks.text: Secondary growth is the increase in the thickness or girth of stems and roots, due to the lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and the cork cambium. It is more prominent in woody perennial plants; herbaceous plants show only primary growth. The cells of the vascular cambium divide and produce new cells on both their outer and inner margins: the outer cells make secondary phloem and the inner cells secondary xylem, and these secondary tissues, particularly the secondary xylem, increase the plant's thickness. Division in the cork cambium also produces cells on both sides, which make new cork. The region of a mature stem outside the vascular cambium, containing secondary phloem, cork cambium and cork, is collectively the bark.

Arrows lead to two stem discs. Upper disc (Apical meristems increase height): Epidermis, Primary phloem, Primary xylem, Vascular cambium. Lower, wider disc (Lateral meristems increase girth): Primary phloem, Secondary phloem, Vascular cambium, Primary xylem, Secondary xylem, with Cork cambium at the outside.

blocks.text: Annual rings form through the seasonal activity of the cambium in trees, influenced by environmental factors, and give two distinct kinds of wood each year: spring wood (early wood) and autumn wood (late wood). The cambium is a meristematic tissue that makes new xylem and phloem. In spring, when conditions are favourable, it is highly active and produces a large volume of xylem with wider vessels, the lighter spring wood. As autumn comes its activity falls and it produces fewer, narrower and denser xylem elements, the darker autumn wood. Spring wood and autumn wood together form one annual ring, and a new ring is added each year, so a tree's age can be determined by dendrochronology. The transition from spring to autumn wood is gradual, but the shift from autumn back to the next spring is abrupt, marking the growth periods clearly; the rings therefore record the age of the tree and the conditions of each growing season, which is valuable for studying long-term climate variability.

blocks.title: Dendrochronology
blocks.text: The scientific method of dating and studying tree rings to analyse past climate conditions and events.

Plants regulate the rates of growth and metabolism in their cells through special chemical messengers, the plant growth regulators or plant hormones. There are five major groups: auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and ethylene.

items: Auxins are indole acetic acid (IAA) and its variants. In the stem they promote cell enlargement in the region behind the apex and cell division in the cambium; in the root they promote growth at very low concentrations but inhibit it at higher ones (as in geotropism), and they promote the growth of roots from cuttings and calluses. They promote bud initiation in shoots (though sometimes they are inhibitory, antagonising cytokinins), apical dominance and fruit growth, can induce parthenocarpy, delay leaf senescence (ageing) in a few species, and inhibit abscission.

Gibberellins are produced in the apical parts of roots and shoots and transported elsewhere; they contain gibberellic acid and more than 110 kinds are known. They promote cell enlargement in the presence of auxins and cell division in the apical meristem and cambium, the bolting of some rosette plants, bud initiation in chrysanthemum callus, leaf and fruit growth (and may induce parthenocarpy), enhance the action of auxins in apical dominance, break bud and seed dormancy, may substitute for red light (so promoting flowering in long-day plants and inhibiting it in short-day plants), and delay leaf senescence in a few species.

Cytokinins are usually produced in roots, young fruits and seeds. They promote cytokinesis in cell division and increase the rates of DNA replication and of RNA and protein synthesis. They promote stem growth by cell division in the apical meristem and cambium, inhibit primary root growth but promote lateral root growth, promote bud initiation and leaf growth, promote fruit growth (rarely inducing parthenocarpy), promote lateral bud growth and break bud dormancy, delay leaf senescence and promote stomatal opening.

Abscisic acid (ABA) is made mainly in mature green leaves, fruits and root caps. It inhibits stem and root growth, notably under physiological stress such as drought and waterlogging, promotes bud and seed dormancy, promotes flowering in short-day plants and inhibits it in long-day plants (antagonising gibberellins), sometimes promotes leaf senescence, promotes abscission, and promotes the closing of stomata under water stress (wilting).

Ethylene is a natural product of plant metabolism. It inhibits stem growth, notably under physiological stress, inhibits root growth, breaks bud dormancy, promotes flowering in pineapple and promotes fruit ripening.
